units: a herder explains that his flock has stopped feeding
he puts the change down to the wetness of the vegetation
a neighbouring herder describes a different reaction in her own animals
the goats crowded against the fence
the herder admits he moved the drinking point
the shade of the hedge made the water too cold to drink
the young animals drank less and lost weight
the herder judges that the fault is his and not the weather's
the neighbour confesses to having made the same mistake before
text: The shepherd told it plainly: his ewes had stopped grazing the moment the wind got up. Wet grass sits heavy, he said, and an uneasy animal chews badly. His neighbour, who keeps goats on the far slope, had watched something else altogether, for her herd had crowded up against the fence and stayed there. At that the shepherd owned up. He had shifted the drinking trough closer to the hedge, and in that shade the water turned cold. Since the move the lambs had been drinking less, they were thinning, and their mothers wore themselves out calling them back. The blame, he decided, lay with a choice of his own making and not with the sky. His neighbour laughed softly at the confession, then admitted she had done exactly the same thing during the cold season before, and to the same end.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: harnessing a draught animal squeezed its throat
that pressure hampered the animal's breathing
the animal could not deliver its full power
craftsmen shifted the bearing onto the shoulders by means of a padded collar
this change raised the load the animal could pull
a head piece served to steer the animal without hurting it
a mouth device protected the drivers from bites
these inventions spread from one valley to the next by copying
text: Harnessing a draught animal once posed a blunt mechanical problem. The strap ran across the throat, and the harder the beast pulled, the tighter it squeezed the windpipe. Breathing failed before the load had properly moved, so a good share of the animal's strength went to waste. The remedy lay in shifting where the pull was borne. Craftsmen carried the bearing onto the shoulders with a padded collar, which left the throat clear under strain and raised the weight a single beast could shift. A supple headpiece was added, so that the animal could be steered without its muzzle being rubbed raw, and a light mouth guard kept the drivers safe from bites during awkward manoeuvres. The design travelled from valley to valley, copied in workshops that knew nothing of whoever had thought of it.

units: birds and mammals feed their young in different ways
chicks leave the egg almost bare
a fine insulating down protects them from the cold
bird parents bring food in from outside the nest
these journeys back and forth are very frequent
young mammals take a food made by their mother
young mammals press against one another to keep their heat
both methods answer the same nutritional need
text: Set a nestful of chicks beside a litter of young mammals and two distinct answers to one and the same requirement come into view. Chicks break out of the egg almost bare; only a thin down keeps them insulated against the cold, and their warmth depends on an adult settling over them. Every mouthful has to be fetched in from outside the nest, which binds the parents to journeys that begin at first light and end only at dusk, back and forth without pause. Among mammals the food is made by the mother herself, so that it stays within reach at all hours and no far errand is called for. The young press close against one another and hold their heat between them while the adults are away. What separates the two, then, is where the food comes from and how freely the parents may move, not the purpose being served, which stays the same in either case.

units: a naturalist made an inventory of the shelters on a wooded slope
a burrow dug under a stump housed a rodent
she never once caught sight of this occupant
a cavity under roots served as a den for a carnivore
birds had built their nests in the cracks of a fallen wall
insects lived under the loose bark of dead trunks
the shelters changed occupant over the course of the season
she handed her notes to a research team, which published them
text: A naturalist settled on a wooded slope and set about listing every shelter the ground there had to offer. She began with the burrows driven into the hillside. One of them opened out beneath a stump and belonged to a rodent she never once set eyes on, for all the hours she gave it. Next came a den wedged under a tangle of roots, lined with hair and twigs, in use by a carnivore of middling size. After that she took in the cracks of a fallen wall, where birds had jammed their nests, and then the loose bark of dead trunks, alive underneath with insects small enough to go unnoticed. What struck her hardest was the turnover: a shelter left empty had been taken over again before the season ran out. She passed her notebooks to a research team, and they published them without delay.

units: you first have to choose a spot sheltered from the wind
the feeding device is fixed high up, out of reach of predators
dry seed is poured into it
salted leftovers are to be avoided
a shallow water container is set beside it
the water must be changed as soon as it turns cloudy
the device must be washed regularly to prevent illness spreading
you have to watch the animals from a distance without going near
the food supply must not be cut off abruptly during the cold season
text: Fancy feeding the birds in the orchard without getting it wrong? Start by finding a corner out of the wind, open enough that a cat cannot climb to it. Fix the feeder well up, a good way off any low branch, then tip in dry seed, never anything salted and never sodden bread. Set a shallow dish of water beside it, a wide saucer will do, and change that water the moment it goes cloudy. Then give the whole lot a scrub in hot water every other week. Droppings build up and pass illness around, and a dirty feeder does more harm than no feeder at all. Watch your visitors from a distance and keep well back, or they will abandon the orchard altogether. One last thing, and it matters: once the cold season has begun, do not cut the food off suddenly, because they have got used to coming and they count on you.

units: the level of a body of water fell after a dry season
a strip of mud joining the shore to the islet was laid bare
land predators took this passage
the nests set on the ground were plundered
the adult birds abandoned the breeding site
part of the colony settled on a steep bank
the site managers had a channel dug to cut the islet off
pairs came back to lay the following season
the original numbers were never recovered
text: A dry season pulled the water level down, and that single drop was enough to undo the colony of birds which had long held the middle islet. As the water drew back it laid bare a tongue of mud running from the shore across to the islet, and the carnivores that prowl the bank were over it on the very first night. Nests built on open ground were ransacked, the eggs lost, and the adults deserted a site they had used year upon year. Some of the colony shifted to a steep rocky bank, harder to reach but wide open to the swell, where hardly a clutch there came to anything. Warned by volunteer watchers, the people managing the site had a narrow channel cut across the mud, so that the islet could no longer be reached on foot. The next season a share of the pairs came back to lay, though the old numbers never returned.

units: a shelter is dug into a bank between roots
brambles hide its entrance
the rains used to flood the passage
the soaked bedding turned bitterly cold for the animal
a second opening was broken through higher up the bank
a dry chamber was dug above the level the water reached
dry grasses cover the floor of this chamber
the old passage now serves to carry the rain away
text: A dark mouth sinks into the bank between the roots, screened so thoroughly by brambles that a walker would pass within a step of it and never notice. The passage runs downward, smooth, polished by fur going through it over and over. In the rains the water used to slide down along the slope and gather at the bottom of it, and the soaked bedding turned bitterly cold under the sleeping animal. So a second mouth was broken open higher up the bank, and from it a shaft climbs to a dry chamber cut above the line the water reaches. Brittle grasses, pulled from the meadow alongside, now cover its floor, and the warmth of the sleeper holds there without any effort at all. The first passage, given up as lodging, carries the rain away instead: it pours in there and comes out lower down, well clear of the bed.

units: the author compares rearing in an enclosed space and rearing on open range
the enclosed space makes every animal easy to pick out and examine
an injury is spotted early there
confinement helps parasites travel
open range builds up the animals' muscle
open range cuts down joint trouble
the scattering of the animals makes health monitoring difficult
the author recommends combining the two systems according to age and season
he asks that the decision rest on measurements and not on convictions
text: Pitting housed rearing against open range rarely settles anything, and the appetite of both camps for a single verdict does the argument more harm than good. Housing has one plain advantage over the rest: every animal can be picked out, weighed and looked over, so that a lesion shows up while it is still small. That same confinement gathers the parasites in and helps them travel through the stock from one animal to the next. Open ground works the other way about. It builds muscle and cuts joint trouble, yet it scatters the animals widely and leaves any health check to chance. A sensible holding therefore runs both systems, sorted by age group and by season, rather than raising either one of them into doctrine. What is still wanting is that the choice be settled on recorded measurements and not on conviction.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who runs a care centre looks after injured animals
she worked as a veterinary assistant before founding her refuge
the refuge occupies an abandoned farm
she feeds the nestlings with forceps at short intervals
she straps up fractured wings and watches them heal
she teaches volunteers to take hold of a frightened animal without hurting it
she enters every arrival in a register
she releases the recovered animals well away from busy roads
she refuses to give a name to the animals taken in
text: The woman who runs the care centre gives her days to creatures that will never be hers. She trained first as a veterinary assistant, learning restraint, splinting and the reading of plates, and only later opened a refuge of her own in a farm that had long stood empty. Her work falls into fixed tasks. She feeds the nestlings with forceps at short intervals, from first light through to dusk. She straps fractured wings, watches the weight come back onto them and adjusts the dressings. She trains volunteers, showing them how to take hold of a frightened animal without hurting it or being bitten. She enters every arrival in a thick register, with the species, the injury and the outcome. And she lets the recovered go well away from busy roads, taking care never to give any of them a name.

units: a documentary book about nocturnal animals is assessed
the opening reports observations carried out in the field
this opening wins the reviewer over
the middle chapters set out measurements from experiments in captivity
this part is judged too dry to read
it nonetheless brings solid knowledge on hearing and orientation
the closing pages give protective recommendations that are too vague
the drawn plates are held to be the great success of the book
the reviewer recommends reading it all the same
text: The book opens with notebooks kept on night watches, and that opening wins you over at once: the author describes long waits, whole evenings that came to nothing, and brief meetings with animals that sensed her well before she could make them out. Then it changes character altogether. The middle chapters set out run after run of measurements taken from animals held in captivity, in prose so dry that the reading bogs down in it. Solid material on hearing and orientation is there to be had, all the same. The closing pages offer a list of protective measures, too broad, sadly, to commit anyone to anything at all. The drawn plates are another matter: they alone repay the trip, so well do they catch posture and movement. It is worth reading all the same, sagging middle and all.
